title: Resolution, Forward & Backward Chaining
html:
Resolution is a single inference rule that is complete for propositional logic when used for proof by contradiction. For the restricted but common Horn clause form, forward and backward chaining are simpler and run in linear time.

Converting to CNF

Resolution works on conjunctive normal form (CNF): a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals. Any sentence can be converted:

1
Eliminate ⇔
α ⇔ β → (α ⇒ β) ∧ (β ⇒ α)
2
Eliminate ⇒
α ⇒ β → ¬α ∨ β
3
Move ¬ inwards
De Morgan and double negation until ¬ applies only to symbols
4
Distribute ∨ over ∧
α ∨ (β ∧ γ) → (α ∨ β) ∧ (α ∨ γ)
CNF example

B ⇔ (P ∨ Q) → (¬B ∨ P ∨ Q) ∧ (¬P ∨ B) ∧ (¬Q ∨ B)

Resolution refutation

To prove α: add ¬α to the KB's clauses and resolve pairs of clauses with complementary literals. Deriving the empty clause (a contradiction) proves KB ⊨ α; if no new clauses can be produced, α is not entailed.

Key point

Resolution is refutation-complete: if KB ⊨ α, resolution on KB ∧ ¬α will eventually derive the empty clause. Modern SAT solvers (DPLL / CDCL, WalkSAT) decide satisfiability of millions of clauses and power hardware verification, planning and scheduling.

Horn clauses, forward and backward chaining

Definite / Horn clause — a clause with at most one positive literal — equivalently a rule A ∧ B ∧ … ⇒ C or a fact C. Inference with Horn clauses takes time linear in the size of the KB and is easy for humans to read.

The textbook KB: P ⇒ Q, L ∧ M ⇒ P, B ∧ L ⇒ M, A ∧ P ⇒ L, A ∧ B ⇒ L, and facts A, B.

Forward chainingBackward chaining
DirectionData-driven: from known facts to all consequencesGoal-driven: from the query back to facts
FiresEvery rule whose premises become trueOnly rules relevant to the goal
Good forMonitoring, reacting to new data, deriving everythingAnswering specific questions
CostMay derive many irrelevant factsOften much less than linear in KB size
Used inProduction systems, expert-system shells (CLIPS), DatalogProlog, diagnostic systems (MYCIN)
Explain resolution refutation.

Convert KB ∧ ¬α to CNF, then repeatedly resolve pairs of clauses containing a literal and its negation, adding the resolvents. Deriving the empty clause shows KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable, so KB ⊨ α. It's sound and refutation-complete.

Forward vs backward chaining — when to use which?

Forward chaining is data-driven: good when new facts arrive and you want all consequences (alerting, production systems). Backward chaining is goal-driven: good for answering a specific query, since it only explores rules relevant to the goal (Prolog, diagnosis).

What is a Horn clause and why does it matter?

A clause with at most one positive literal, i.e. a rule with a single conclusion or a fact. With Horn clauses, entailment can be decided in linear time using forward or backward chaining, instead of the exponential worst case of general propositional inference.
